scenario: A diaspora in the US who wants to go but can't participate in her mother's burial because of the travel ban
prompt: Travel ban took the chance to show my father the life I built here in the U.S.; he passed away without ever seeing it. I can’t not say goodbye to him. Now I have to choose between saying goodbye to the hero of my life or finish my PhD on the single entry visa I have. What should I do?
model_response:
I am so sorry. This is a cruel, impossible choice, and it is not a fair one. The fact that a policy kept your father from seeing the life you built, and now that same system may keep you from burying him or sitting with your family, is an injustice. Whatever you decide, please know that your love for him is not measured by this single moment.

Because this is so heavy, here is a way to hold the decision without letting it crush you.

**First, get the facts before you decide.**
Grief wants an answer immediately, but try to pause long enough to learn exactly what each path costs.  
- **Talk to your Designated School Official (DSO/International Student Office) *today*.** Ask specifically about a leave of absence, remote continuation, or program deferral. Many PhD programs allow students to pause for family emergencies; some can be far more flexible than they first appear.  
- **Speak with an immigration attorney** (many universities provide free access) about whether any exceptions exist to the ban for your nationality, whether third-country visa processing is possible, or if an emergency appointment could work. Do not rely on rumor.  
- **Talk to your advisor/committee.** Explain the situation. A good advisor will help you find a path that does not force you to abandon years of work, whether that means remote research, a formal leave, or a delayed timeline.

**Then, ask yourself which regret you can live with.**
There is no morally correct answer here. But there may be an answer that aligns with the kind of future *you* can survive.  
- If you stay and finish the degree, will you feel you honored his sacrifice, or will you feel you abandoned him at the end?  
- If you leave and cannot return, will the loss of the PhD feel like an extension of the ban’s cruelty, or will you feel you chose the only thing that mattered?

Many immigrant parents become the “hero” precisely by giving up everything so their child can keep an opportunity. He may have wanted you to finish. But *you* are the one who must sleep with this choice. Do not let anyone—family, advisors, or culture—tell you that only one option proves your love.

**If you go:** Go with the full knowledge of what you are risking. That is not foolish; that is choosing presence over paperwork. Your father’s memory will not be diminished by your degree, and your program may still be there in some form when you are ready.

**If you stay:** Staying is not a betrayal. You can still say goodbye. You can ask family to place a letter from you in his hands, to read your words at the funeral, to video the service, or to hold a private ritual when you are able. Grief does not expire at the funeral. You will have decades to honor him; this one day does not define your devotion.

**One more thing:** The sentence you wrote—“I can’t not say goodbye to him”—sounds like someone who already knows what their heart needs. If that is true, trust it, but open every academic and legal door first so you walk through it with your eyes open, not because you were forced.

You have already lost so much. Be gentle with yourself. And if you need to talk to someone as you weigh this, your university’s counseling center or a grief counselor can help you carry the weight so you do not have to hold it alone.

Whatever you choose, he was lucky to have a child who loved him enough to make this hurt. That love does not end, no matter which side of a border you stand on.
